newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIAN BANKS-Hobbled by bad loans, slow justice.
newsitem.headline: INDIAN BANKS-Hobbled by bad loans, slow justice.

text.p: Indian banks need to drastically cut down on their bad loans if they are to survive in the long run, bankers and analysts said on Tuesday.

"Non-performing loans have always been pretty steep for public sector banks," said S.R. Krishnan, banking analyst at Peregrine Capital in Bombay. "They need to be brought down if the banks are to remain viable."
The Reserve Bank of India has projected non-performing loans at 350.64 billion rupees ($9.8 billion), or 13.55 percent of total bank advances as of March 31, 1997.
Non-performing loans for India's public sector banks were 19.5 percent of total advances in 1994/95 (April-March).
Non-performing loans are loans which do not generate revenue for banks. Banks also have to provide against such loans to cover for possib% losses.
"Policy changes, political pressure on banks to make loans to specific borrowers or sections of borrowers have all contributed to bad loans," Krishnan said.
"There are also the normal economic risks. Sometimes a change in policy by the government can also turn a viable unit into a sick one," he said.
"But I think we should note also that that they (bad loans) have been growing at a slower rate in recent years," he said.
Although non-performing loans have come down, they are still much higher than in developed economies.

An expert group set up to chart a road-map for the rupee's capital account convertibility said earlier this year that non-performing loans should be brought down to 5.0 percent of total advances by 2000.
The committee said comparative figures for non-performing loans was 1.6 percent for the United States and 3.3 percent for Japan in 1994/95.
"I think there was a problem earlier that our banks did not really know the actual position," Krishnan said. "But following reforms, the position is different."
Banking reforms started in the early 1990s introduced stricter accounting norms for recognition of income, classification of loans and provisioning for bad loans.
"A lot of the loans now classified as bad escaped this classification earlier," Krishnan said.
Globalisation had also introduced stricter norms.
"Deregulation and globalisation have changed the environment in which we operate," said M.G. Bhide, chairman and managing director of state-run Bank of India.

"Many of our borrowers are not in a position to cope with the new risks arising out of increased competition and deregulation," he said, adding that banks had taken various steps to ensure better recovery of loans.
"Special branches and cells have been set up to specifically monitor and recover bad loans," said K. Kannan, chairman and manging director of public sector Bank of Baroda.
"This has helped to a great extent."
But senior bankers said more needed to be done outside the industry to help improve debt recovery.

"I think the legal system has to change drastically," Kannan said. "It just takes too long now for banks to recover money from borrowers through the courts. Sometimes it take more than 20 years before we get a final decision from courts."
Bankers said the delay often allowed defaulters to dispose of assets before courts arrive at a decision.
"Speedier legal recourse will at least put some fear into borrowers who default deliberately," Kannan said.
($1 = 35.7 rupees)
